Nathan Yang^2^ · **H. Sherry Zhang**^3^ · Dianne Cook^1^ ::: ::: {.affil} ^1^Monash University ^2^Duke University ^3^The University of Texas at Austin [sugarglider is a Google Summer of Code project]{.gsoc} ::: ::: ::: {.header-hex} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](poster_files/figure-pdf/header-glyph-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.pcols} ::: {.pcol} ::: {.card .lead} ## Why glyph maps? Environmental data are often **many time series at many locations**: weather stations, river gauges, air-quality monitors, satellite grid cells. Small multiples lose the geography; animated maps lose the time series. A **glyph map** keeps both: each location's time series is drawn as a small plot (a *glyph*) placed at that location on the map, so you can read **local** seasonal shape and **global** spatial pattern at once [(Wickham et al., 2012)]{.cite}. ::: ::: {.card} ## How a glyph is built Each glyph has two coordinate systems: **major** (where on the map) and **minor** (the time series inside the glyph). ![](figures/diagram-transformation.png){width=78%} The minor axes are rescaled to $[-1, 1]$ and placed by a linear transformation: $$ \begin{aligned} x &= x_{\text{major}} + \tfrac{\text{width}}{2}\, x_{\text{minor}} \\ y &= y_{\text{major}} + \tfrac{\text{height}}{2}\, y_{\text{minor}} \end{aligned} $$ **Design choices that matter:** - **Global vs local rescale:** global lets you compare *magnitude* across sites; local makes the *shape* at each site visible. - **Reference boxes and lines** frame each glyph and give a baseline, which counters the Zöllner illusion of drifting lines. - **Glyph size** trades detail against overlap. ::: ::: {.card} ## A brief lineage ::: {.timeline} [2012]{.yr} **GGally::glyphs()**: computes glyph coordinates as a data frame that you draw yourself with `geom_path()`. [2023]{.yr} **cubble::geom_glyph()**: makes the glyph a ggplot2 *layer*, with `x_major`, `x_minor`, `y_major`, `y_minor` as aesthetics. [2026]{.yr} **sugarglider** [(R Journal)]{.cite}: adds **ribbon** and **segment** glyphs, which show an *interval* (e.g. daily min to max) over time, plus legends and themes. ::: ::: ::: {.card} ## Which one should I use? | | **GGally** | **cubble** | **sugarglider** | |:--|:--:|:--:|:--:| | Interface | `glyphs()` → data frame | ggplot2 layer | ggplot2 layer | | Glyph geometry | line | line | **ribbon, segment** | | Reference box & line | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Global / local rescale | via `y_scale` | ✓ | ✓ | | Polar glyphs | ✓ | ✓ | – | | Glyph legend & theme | – | – | ✓ | | Spatio-temporal data structure | – | ✓ | via cubble | | Interactive (ggiraph, leaflet) | – | via crosstalk | ✓ | ::: ::: ::: {.pcol} ::: {.card} ## GGally: the original `glyphs()` returns the transformed coordinates (`gx`, `gy`, `gid`); `add_ref_boxes()` and `add_ref_lines()` add the frames. Rescalers `range01()`, `rescale11()`, `mean0()`, `max1()` and `min0()` control what each glyph compares, and `polar = TRUE` wraps the glyph into a circle. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(GGally) gly <- glyphs(nasa, x_major = "long", x_minor = "day", y_major = "lat", y_minor = "surftemp") ggplot(gly, aes(gx, gy, group = gid)) + add_ref_boxes(gly) + add_ref_lines(gly) + geom_path() ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](poster_files/figure-pdf/ggally-map-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.card} ## cubble: glyphs as a ggplot2 layer `geom_glyph()`, `geom_glyph_box()` and `geom_glyph_line()` take the major and minor variables as **aesthetics**, so glyph maps compose with any other layer (base maps, points, facets). They take a `polar`, `global_rescale`, `width`/`height` and `x_scale`/`y_scale` arguments. cubble's spatio-temporal data structure makes the wrangling easy: summarise in the **temporal** face, then `unfold()` the coordinates in before plotting. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(cubble) climate_aus |> face_temporal() |> group_by(month = lubridate::month(date)) |> summarise(tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> unfold(long, lat) |> ggplot(aes(x_major = long, x_minor = month, y_major = lat, y_minor = tmax)) + geom_glyph_box() + geom_glyph_line() + geom_glyph() ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](poster_files/figure-pdf/cubble-map-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: [Southern stations swing strongly from summer to winter; tropical stations in the north stay hot all year with only a shallow mid-year dip.]{.takeaway} ::: ::: ::: {.pcol} ::: {.card .feature} ## sugarglider: intervals, not just lines sugarglider began as a **Google Summer of Code** project. A single line hides **variability**. Many environmental summaries are *ranges*: daily min–max temperature, quantile bands, uncertainty intervals. **sugarglider** adds two glyph geometries for them: ::: {.two-up} ::: {} **`geom_glyph_ribbon()`**
a band from `ymin_minor` to `ymax_minor` ::: ::: {} **`geom_glyph_segment()`**
a segment from `y_minor` to `yend_minor` ::: ::: plus the scaffolding for a readable map: `add_glyph_boxes()`, `add_ref_lines()`, `add_glyph_legend()` (an enlarged, labelled glyph to read the scale) and `theme_glyph()`. ::: ::: {.card .feature} ## sugarglider in action ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(sugarglider) aus_temp |> ggplot(aes(x_major = long, y_major = lat, x_minor = month, ymin_minor = tmin, ymax_minor = tmax)) + add_glyph_boxes() + add_ref_lines() + add_glyph_legend() + geom_glyph_ribbon() + theme_glyph() ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](poster_files/figure-pdf/ribbon-map-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: [Wet tropical stations have flat, narrow bands; inland stations show wide daily ranges and deep winter dips.]{.takeaway} ::: ::: {.card .feature} ## Global vs local rescale ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](poster_files/figure-pdf/rescale-maps-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: [**Segment glyphs, two scalings.** Global scaling compares magnitudes across Australia; local scaling reveals each station's own seasonal shape.]{.caption} ::: ::: ::: {.pcol} ::: {.card .feature} ## Anatomy of a sugarglider map ![](figures/glyphmap-layers.png){width=100%} Every layer is its own function, so you add only what you need: a base map (`geom_sf()`), glyph boxes, reference lines, the ribbon or segment glyphs, and an optional legend glyph. ::: ::: {.card .lead .takehome} ## Take-home 1. A glyph map shows each site's **temporal shape** and the **spatial pattern** in one plot. 2. If your summary is a **range** (min–max, quantiles, uncertainty), use sugarglider's **ribbon** or **segment** glyphs. 3. Use **global** rescaling to compare magnitude across sites and **local** rescaling to compare shape. 4. All three packages work with **ggplot2**, so you can add base maps, colour and facets as usual. ::: ::: {.card .getstarted} ## Get started ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages(c("sugarglider", "cubble", "GGally")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](poster_files/figure-pdf/qr-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.refs} Wickham, Hofmann, Wickham & Cook (2012). Glyph-maps for visually exploring temporal patterns in climate data and models. *Environmetrics* 23(5), 382–393. [doi:10.1002/env.2152](https://doi.org/10.1002/env.2152)
Zhang, Cook, Laa, Langrené & Menéndez (2024). cubble: An R package for organizing and wrangling multivariate spatio-temporal data. *J. Stat. Softw.* 110(7). [doi:10.18637/jss.v110.i07](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v110.i07)
